summary: Children aged 9–11 acquire and correctly USE the technical vocabulary of electric circuits (circuit, component, cell, battery, current, voltage, resistance, conductor, insulator, switch, series, parallel) while describing, drawing and designing real working circuits. Words are tied to handled components and observed behaviour; the abstract quantity definitions (current = charge flow; voltage = energy per charge; resistance in ohms) are deferred to later, KS3, study — here the words name things children can see and do. In England's KS2, pupils investigate SERIES circuits only, so 'parallel' is taught as a named contrast term, not an investigated configuration. Priority is fencing the confusable pairs (cell/battery, series/parallel, conductor/insulator, current/voltage) through active production rather than front-loading all twelve words at once.
misconceptions: Cell vs battery conflation — calling a single cell 'a battery'; a battery is two or more cells connected together.
Using 'current', 'voltage', 'energy' and 'electricity' interchangeably — they name different things (the flow, the push, what's transferred, the general phenomenon).
Mixing up 'series' and 'parallel', or thinking KS2 circuits can be parallel (KS2 is series only).
Thinking 'component' means only the special parts (bulb, buzzer) and not the cell or wires.
Carrying 'current is used up / flows out one end' talk into the vocabulary — the words should support a complete-loop, conserved-current picture, not undermine it.

activities.title: Label a real circuit and lift the contrast
steps: Build or examine a simple working series circuit (cells, wires, a bulb or buzzer, a switch).
Pin or write a vocabulary tag onto each part and behaviour: cell, battery, wire, bulb, switch, current, voltage, component.

For each confusable word, reveal a child-friendly meaning plus a non-example that fences its boundary: 'cell — one power source; join two or more and you've got a BATTERY'; 'conductor — lets electricity through' beside 'insulator — blocks it'; 'current — what flows round the loop' beside 'voltage — the push from the cells'.
State aloud why the non-example is NOT the term (e.g. why a single cell is not a battery).
activities.insight: Each non-example snaps a fuzzy word into a sharp boundary — the child stops saying 'battery' for a single cell and 'voltage' for the flow, because the contrast is attached to a real part they can see and handle.

activities.title: Make the words do their job (words that enact)
steps: Work with a small circuit where dynamic words change what happens: add a cell in series, facing the same way as the others (more voltage), and watch the bulb brighten, using a bulb rated for the extra voltage; name the change using the word 'voltage'.

Reconfigure the loop between a single loop (series) and branches (parallel) and describe, using the words, what is different about the PATH — treating parallel as the named contrast, not a circuit to investigate at KS2.
Say how 'resistance' shows itself: adding a component with more resistance into the single loop (in series) makes the bulb dimmer; resistance limits the current, it does not break the circuit.
activities.insight: The relational words (current, voltage, resistance, series vs parallel) name behaviours, not just definitions — seeing 'more voltage → brighter' and 'series vs parallel → different path' maps each word onto something observable.

activities.title: Describe and design a working circuit, in role
steps: Given a working torch or series circuit, describe out loud how it works using current, voltage, resistance, series and component, saying what each word is DOING, not its dictionary meaning.

Aim for a description that places each term in its correct role, e.g. 'the cell provides the voltage that pushes a current around the series circuit; the current flows through each component — bulb, switch, wire; the bulb has resistance, which is why it glows and limits the current.'
Design a simple series circuit to meet a stated goal (e.g. a circuit with a switch that turns a buzzer on and off), sketch it, and describe your design using the correct vocabulary.
Then adjust the description for a new configuration: what would change in your words if the bulbs were in parallel (branches) instead of one single loop (series)?

Answer probing questions: 'You said the current flows — what is the voltage doing, is it also flowing or something different?' and 'This circuit has two bulbs in one single loop — is it series or parallel, and how do the words tell you?'
activities.insight: Correct USE places each term in its right role in the sentence; a child who has only memorised definitions can recite them yet still swap current for voltage or call any multi-bulb circuit 'parallel'. Threading the words through an accurate live description and through a circuit the child designs is the real evidence of understanding.

activities.title: Sort, match and complete circuit descriptions
steps: Match each word to its component or meaning (e.g. switch ↔ opens/closes the loop; insulator ↔ blocks electricity).
Sort materials or components into conductor vs insulator, and sort circuit features into series vs parallel.
Complete fill-the-gap circuit descriptions such as 'the ___ pushes the ___ round the loop' using the correct terms.
activities.insight: Sorting and completing descriptions consolidates the vocabulary and checks that boundaries between confusable terms hold, especially conductor/insulator and series/parallel.

checkQuestion: Here's a torch circuit that's working. Describe out loud how it works, using the words current, voltage, resistance, series and component correctly — tell me what each word is doing in your description, not its dictionary meaning.
checkAnswer: Uses the terms in a working description, e.g. 'the cell provides the voltage that pushes a current around the series circuit; the current flows through each component — bulb, switch, wire; the bulb has resistance, which is why it glows and why it limits the current.' The terms sit in their correct roles in context, not recited as isolated definitions.
